analysis.one_liner: Loosens SEC registration, disclosure, and audit rules for companies raising money from investors.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 212-205 on March 8, 2024 with every voting Republican in favor and every voting Democrat opposed, but the Senate never voted and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill rolls back a series of Securities and Exchange Commission rules covering how companies raise money. It would exempt small stock offerings from registration, triple the size of offerings that can skip full registration to $150 million a year, let companies with up to $1.5 billion in revenue sell stock with reduced public disclosure for longer, expand the legal definition of who may be sold unregistered securities, and let retail mutual funds and retirement plans route more money into lightly regulated private investment funds. Supporters framed it as helping small businesses and startups raise capital; critics said it strips away investor protections. It passed the House on a party-line vote but never received a Senate vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies raising money — especially startups, mid-sized growth firms, and private fund managers — gain easier, cheaper access to capital with fewer registration filings, audits, and public disclosures. Venture capital funds can grow to 15 times the current size while keeping their regulatory exemptions, crowdfunding portals shed liability and anti-money-laundering duties, and securities brokers gain new safe harbors for selling private placements. Retail investors also gain nominal new avenues: they can invest in unregistered private offerings after a self-attestation or a 10% income/asset cap, and gig workers can receive company equity as compensation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Companies raising capital and private fund managers

how_it_helps.text: It raises the revenue limit for 'emerging growth company' status to $1.5 billion and extends the reduced-disclosure period to seven years, letting larger companies sell stock with fewer public disclosures [S4].

It raises the venture capital fund exemption caps from $10 million to $150 million in capital and from 250 to 600 investors, allowing larger funds to operate without the filings, audits, and investor-communication rules that apply to other investment firms [S4].

It exempts offerings of up to $250,000 from securities registration, triples the Regulation A+ offering cap from $50 million to $150 million, and expands crowdfunding limits while exempting crowdfunding portals from certain anti-money-laundering requirements and most liability for misstatements [S4].
It creates safe harbors exempting 'private placement brokers' and 'finders' from broker registration and bars states from imposing greater requirements on them [S4].

It expands who qualifies as an 'accredited investor' — including anyone who attests they understand private-market risks or invests no more than 10% of their income or net assets — and lets closed-end funds put retail shareholder money into private investment funds [S4].

analysis.who_pays: The costs fall on investors and on the public's ability to see what companies are doing: weaker disclosure requirements for companies with up to $1.5 billion in revenue, exempted brokers and crowdfunding portals facing reduced liability and anti-money-laundering duties, and a wider door for ordinary savers to move money into unregistered private offerings that carry less transparency and fewer legal remedies. State regulators also lose the ability to oversee secondary trading in some securities.

drawbacks.text: Crowdfunding portals would be exempt from anti-money-laundering recordkeeping and reporting requirements and from liability for material misstatements or omissions unless they knowingly engage in fraud [S4], shifting risk onto small investors who buy through these portals.

The bill lets anyone become an 'accredited investor' simply by signing a two-page attestation that they understand the risks of private offerings [S4][S5], removing the income and net-worth guardrails that currently keep inexperienced savers out of high-risk unregistered investments.

States would be barred from imposing registration, audit, or reporting requirements on private-placement brokers and finders, or from regulating off-exchange secondary trading of securities of issuers that post basic financial information [S4][S5], preempting state investor-protection laws.

The eligibility ceiling for 'emerging growth company' reduced-disclosure treatment would rise from $1 billion to $1.5 billion in annual revenues and last up to seven years [S4], letting very large companies sell stock with less public disclosure than current law requires.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill contains a few genuinely low-cost modernizations — electronic delivery of required investor documents with an opt-out for paper, and letting 403(b) school and charity retirement plans use pooled investment trusts — that reduce costs without weakening core protections. But the bulk of the bill relaxes the disclosure and liability rules that protect investors in securities markets, in ways whose benefits accrue mainly to issuers, private fund managers, and financial intermediaries. The honest trade-off is modest administrative savings and somewhat easier small-company fundraising against a broad reduction in the transparency and accountability that lets investors know what they are buying and gives them recourse when misled.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it on a near party-line vote, but it went to the Senate Banking Committee, never got a floor vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: The House Financial Services Committee approved the bill 28-21 on April 26, 2023, and it was reported to the floor on July 17, 2023 [S7].

On March 8, 2024, the House rejected a Democratic motion to recommit 205-213 with every voting Democrat in favor and every voting Republican opposed (roll call 77), then passed the bill 212-205 with every voting Republican in favor and every voting Democrat opposed (roll call 78) [S8][S9].
The Senate received the bill on March 11, 2024 and referred it to the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee, where it stayed with no further action [S7].
The bill received no cosponsors in the House [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary investors in securities markets, because the reduced disclosure and liability protections they rely on were never enacted; securities issuers and financial firms gained nothing either.

sides.party_line_note: The final vote split perfectly by party: 212 Republicans in favor, 205 Democrats opposed, with no crossover on either side [S8].

industries.industry: Venture capital and private equity funds
industries.note: The bill raises the venture fund exemption caps from $10 million to $150 million and from 250 to 600 investors, counts secondary-market and fund-of-fund stakes as qualifying investments, and lets closed-end retail funds invest in private funds — a large new pool of money for private markets [S4].

industries.industry: Investment banks, brokers, and private-placement intermediaries
industries.note: The bill exempts private-placement brokers and finders from broker registration, protects research reports on all issuers from registration treatment, and lowers the bar for expedited shelf offerings by 'well-known seasoned issuers' — reducing compliance costs for intermediaries and issuers alike [S4].

industries.industry: Crowdfunding portals and Reg A issuers
industries.note: Crowdfunding portals gain exemption from anti-money-laundering recordkeeping and from liability for material misstatements unless committed knowingly, and the Regulation A+ offering cap triples to $150 million — more revenue with less accountability to the small investors on the other side [S4].

industries.industry: Emerging growth companies and large issuers
industries.note: Companies gain cheaper, less-disclosed access to public and private capital markets, but take on less scrutiny in return; the benefit to the companies comes at the cost of information available to the public [S4].

industries.industry: Banks and trust companies offering collective investment trusts
industries.note: The bill lets 403(b) retirement plans for school, charity, and church employees invest in bank collective investment trusts and insurance company separate accounts, expanding a fee-gathering product line [S4].
The bill preempts state rules on private-placement brokers, finders, and off-exchange secondary trading, stripping state regulators of authority over growing segments of the securities market [S4].

The bill extends the employee stock-compensation exemption to independent contractors, letting gig workers receive equity in the platforms they serve — a real benefit to those workers, delivered through the same private-market channels [S4].
